items.summary: The existence of humans on Malta, a tiny Mediterranean island, during the Mesolithic period is puzzling. items.summary: The tropics cover less than one-third of Earth's surface but are home to more than half of all known species. items.title: Small ants that evict coffee pests may gain reproductive boost while protecting crops
items.summary: Ants are known allies in the fight against coffee pests known as coffee berry borers. Now, a discovery made by Jonathan "Jonno" Morris while he was a University of Michigan graduate student has revealed there may be a new dimension to this protection.

items.title: Social amoebae form nanotube networks linking multiple cells
items.summary: Social amoebae are unicellular organisms that act in concert, requiring extensive communication. Pierre Stallforth and colleagues studied modes of communication among cells of the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, using fluorescent labeling and various imaging techniques.

items.title: 'Rivers in the sky' influence marine heat waves
items.summary: Long, narrow bands of moving moisture in the sky, known as atmospheric rivers, contribute to heat waves in the marine environment, according to a new study published in Nature Communications by researchers from Duke University's Nicholas School of the Environment. items.title: Elephant vaccine shows first signs of protection against deadly virus

items.title: Falling birth rates mean schools are closing—affecting whole communities
items.summary: As another academic year ends, some schools will be closing their doors permanently because of declining numbers of children. In England, declining birth rates over the past decade have led to more than 100 schools, predominantly in urban areas, closing permanently.

items.title: US residents near small rivers face disproportionately high future flood risks
items.summary: An international team, including Kumamoto University and its partner institutions, has found severe flood risks and high climate-adaptation costs for U.S. small rivers.
